description: Learn how to use view transitions to communicate meaning during navigation, loading, and content changes in a Next.js app.

In web apps, route changes replace the entire page at once. One set of elements disappears, another appears, with no visual connection between them. A user selects a photo thumbnail to view it in detail on another page. They are the same image, but nothing on screen communicates that.

Apps that need these transitions typically rely on complex animation libraries that manage mount/unmount lifecycles, track element positions across routes, and coordinate timing manually, to animate how elements enter, exit, and move between states.

React's `<ViewTransition>` component integrates with the browser's [View Transitions API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/View_Transition_API) to handle this declaratively. You name the elements that should persist, and the browser animates between their old and new positions.

This guide walks through four patterns that cover the most common cases: morphing shared elements, animating loading states, adding directional navigation, and crossfading content within the same route.

---
title: Designing view transitions
description: Learn how to use view transitions to communicate meaning during navigation, loading, and content changes in a Next.js app.
nav_title: View transitions
---

In web apps, route changes replace the entire page at once. One set of elements disappears, another appears, with no visual connection between them. A user selects a photo thumbnail to view it in detail on another page. They are the same image, but nothing on screen communicates that.

Apps that need these transitions typically rely on complex animation libraries that manage mount/unmount lifecycles, track element positions across routes, and coordinate timing manually, to animate how elements enter, exit, and move between states.

React's `<ViewTransition>` component integrates with the browser's [View Transitions API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/View_Transition_API) to handle this declaratively. You name the elements that should persist, and the browser animates between their old and new positions.

This guide walks through four patterns that cover the most common cases: morphing shared elements, animating loading states, adding directional navigation, and crossfading content within the same route.

Done. Build and typecheck both pass cleanly.

**What was added:**

- **`app/page.tsx`** — Wrapped the page in a directional `<ViewTransition>` (enter/exit keyed by `nav-forward` / `nav-back`). The Suspense fallback gets `exit="slide-down"` and the grid content gets `enter="slide-up"` for a smooth skeleton handoff.
- **`app/ProductGrid.tsx`** — Each thumbnail wrapped in `<ViewTransition name={`product-image-${slug}`} share="morph" default="none">` so it pairs with the hero on the detail page. Each card `<Link>` carries `transitionTypes={['nav-forward']}` to tag forward navigations.
- **`app/product/[slug]/page.tsx`** — Same directional `<ViewTransition>` wrapper. Hero wrapped with the matching `name={`product-image-${slug}`} share="morph" default="none">`. Back link carries `transitionTypes={['nav-back']}`. Product details Suspense uses the same `slide-down`/`slide-up` pair.
- **`app/globals.css`** — CSS recipes for `.morph` (mid-flight blur), `.nav-forward` / `.nav-back` (60px horizontal slide + fade), and `.slide-down` / `.slide-up` (vertical handoff). `::view-transition { pointer-events: none }` keeps the page clickable mid-transition. The `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` block zeros every view-transition animation duration and delay, so reduced-motion users get instant swaps.

**How the patterns compose during navigation:**

1. Grid → detail (`nav-forward`): page slides left/right via `.nav-forward`, and the colored image morphs from its grid cell into the hero via the shared `product-image-{slug}` name.
2. Detail → grid (back link → `nav-back`): mirror slide in the opposite direction, hero morphs back to its card position.
3. Suspense swap (100 ms server delay on the detail page): `DetailsSkeleton` fades out with `slide-down` while `ProductDetails` fades up with `slide-up`.
4. Browser back/forward, `router.refresh()`, or any transition without a tagged type falls through `default: "none"`, so only intentional transitions animate.

Patterns and CSS recipes follow the official guide at `node_modules/next/dist/docs/01-app/02-guides/view-transitions.md`.
